scenes.title: Watch the whole story first

beats.text: Consider a crate on a rough floor. A rope pulls it sideways, not hard enough... friction holds it.
A friend leans on the crate, pressing straight down. The floor is squeezed harder, so it grips harder. Still no movement.
Instead, the friend pulls a second rope upwards at an angle. Part of that pull drags the crate along... part of it lifts, so the floor grips less.
And now it slides. Same extra force, different direction, different result.

scenes.title: Why the extra force matters

beats.text: Vertically the crate does not move, so R is whatever balances the vertical forces.
Press down: R grows, and since f max equals mu R, the limit grows too.
Pull up: R shrinks, and so does the limit.
beats.caption: Smaller R, smaller f max

beats.text: An angled force does both: a horizontal part pulls along, a vertical part changes R. We resolve it into those two parts.
beats.caption: Angled force: along, and up

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The full question. A crate of mass four kilograms rests on a rough horizontal floor, coefficient of friction zero point two five. Take g as ten.
A horizontal rope pulls it to the right with nine newtons. It stays in contact with the floor.
Part a: a second force of eight newtons presses vertically down on the crate. Does it move?
Part b: instead, the eight newtons pulls at thirty degrees above the horizontal, to the right. Find the friction and the acceleration.
Which case do you expect to move? Take a moment.

scenes.title: Part a: pressing down

beats.text: Part a. Vertically: R up; the weight m g and the eight newton push down. R minus m g minus eight equals zero.
The weight is four times ten, forty. So R is forty plus eight: forty-eight newtons, more than the weight.
The limit: f max equals mu R.
Zero point two five times forty-eight: twelve newtons.
The rope pulls with nine. Nine is less than twelve, so friction can hold it: the crate stays at rest.
Horizontally: X minus f equals m a.
Nine minus f equals four times zero, so friction is nine newtons and the acceleration is zero.

scenes.title: Part b: resolve the angled pull

beats.text: Part b. The eight newtons pulls at thirty degrees above the horizontal. Draw its triangle: the force is the sloping side.
The horizontal part is F cos theta.
Eight cos thirty is four root three, about six point nine newtons, along the floor.
The vertical part is F sine theta.
Eight sine thirty is four newtons, upwards.
These two components now replace the angled force. Never count the eight newtons and its parts together.

scenes.title: Part b: the new reaction and limit

beats.text: Vertically: R and the four newton lift up, weight down. R plus V equals m g.
R plus four is forty, so R is thirty-six newtons: less than the weight this time.
The limit: f max equals mu R.
Zero point two five times thirty-six: nine newtons.
Along the floor: the rope gives nine, the component four root three. About fifteen point nine newtons, more than nine.
So it slides, and friction sits at its maximum, nine newtons.

scenes.title: Part b: Newton’s second law

beats.text: Newton’s second law along the floor: resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Rope plus component minus friction equals four a.
The nines cancel: four root three equals four a.
So a is root three, about one point seven three metres per second squared, to the right.
The rope alone could not move the crate. The angled pull did it twice over: it pulled along, and it made the floor grip less.

scenes.title: What would change pulling straight up?

beats.text: What if the eight newtons pulled straight up? R would be forty minus eight: thirty-two newtons.
The limit: zero point two five times thirty-two, eight newtons. Nine beats eight, so it slides with no extra pull along the floor.
